title: Buddy Bolden's Blues and the word twist
summary: Morton's short Bolden strain and the earlier use of the twist in older songs.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues

blocks.x: What about, this, Buddy Bowden's blues? Jelly must have written that or must have had it in his head long before he had it.
he had it in his head. Never, the, the little strain, it was a very short strain. That was it. See?
That's all it is too. But it's a great strain.

Well, he worked it up. Of course, there were others that worked it up into a, an instrumental piece, you know, the St. Louis Tickle uses it as an instrumental, they use a strain, but not, not like Telly Rhodes exactly. They worked it up on their arrangement, Barney and Seymour. But, to work it up and put the words to it that, that he did, some, some like, what were being used around him, some I think he cooked up himself. They, I had to laugh about the use of words, you know, this, this twist, when the dance came out, the twist, when everything was supposed to be new, that's what's new, the twist of dance, but, Jelly Roll has it in, in, what is that?
No, no, is it, Mama, Mama, take a look at Sis, she's out in the alley doing the double twist?

And they say, Tony Jackson used it in Michigan Water Blues, and then, while I was still in New Orleans, it was a kind of a, kind of a joke or a gag around town, you know, and they say, well, you know what the, what the boys are asking the girls when they want them to dance now at these dancers? They say, no, so, well, they say, hey kid, is your frame engaged for the next twist? Yeah. So, there's nothing new under the sun.
